speechtext: Mr. Chairman, after listening to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) this afternoon one would think that the government had ended the depression, that its great wisdom in dealing with the affairs of the country had resulted in some remarkable salvation of conditions generally. What are the facts? At the special session of the house, a few weeks after the right hon. gentleman came into office, we were asked to vote $20,000,000 for unemployment relief. The Prime Minister himself estimated that we had at that time something like 117,000 unemployed in Canada, and said that, if the policies of the government had the effect which the government believed they were going to have, they hoped they would not have to ask parliament for further unemployment relief in another year; that the numbers of unemployed would gradually diminish. But what has happened? At the present time we have over 800,000 unemployed in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is not correct.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) told us the other evening that the number of people on relief ran up to over 1,300,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I am sorry to interject but I thought I made myself quite plain. The number receiving relief for varying periods, not constant, including men old and young, women old and young, middle-aged and infants in arms amounts to approximately 1,300,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is just what I have said. Let us leave alone the question of dependents and take the actual number of unemployed-

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I never said the number of unemployed was 800,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman did not, he did not take exception to my statement when I said that the number of unemployed had been given as such by the government's representative in Great Britain. Only two tw three months ago, Mr. Howard Ferguson announced in London that the total

number of unemployed in Canada, at that time was 800,000. No exception has been taken to that statement made by Canada's representative in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The figure was not 800,000 unemployed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: What was it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That 800,000 were then receiving relief.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I think that was the number of unemployed, and I think it will be found to be so. I took great care to note what the High Commissioner for Canada said at the time. I say further that, if the minister will give to this house an official statement of the total number of unemployed, he will find that figure is within the number. I do not think the government will deny that for one minute.
When the Prime Minister endeavours to have it appear that the course which he has taken has been a course Which has saved the country, I want the committee to have a realization of the facts of the situation. The country to-day is in a worse position than it has been at any time since the present administration took office, and, I think, at any time in the history of Canada. That is the situation as it exists to-d)ay. The Prime Minister would have us believe that the wisdom of the executive had been the means of saving the situation.
The Prime Minister has sought to have us believe that it is an impossible thing for a government to provide for emergencies by fixing any definite amount in the estimates, that because no one can foresee what is going to take place, therefore, that the ministry must be given unlimited power to spend whatever moneys it pleases. From the time of confederation up to the present, has there been any occasion, except that which has occurred in this parliament, where a free hand was given to the ministry in the matter of expending public moneys? No one expects the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour, or anybody else, to come to parliament and say:	We need precisely so many hundreds
of thousands, or so many millions of dollars, for a specific purpose; this is exactly what is going to be required this year. That is not what is asked of the ministry. But the ministry is asked and is expected to make some estimate, and it may make that estimate as large or as small as it pleases. All that the ministry is expected to do is to say to parliament: We believe that so much will be required this year for such and such purposes,

Relief Act, 1933-Mr. Mackenzie King
and we base our estimate upon the following grounds which would then be enumerated. We are now in the fourth session of this parliament, and we have had this method of proceeding for nearly three years. Had the ministry adopted from the outset the course which we on this side proposed, it would have been possible for the government to have said to us to-day: We believe that $20,000,000 is all that will be required for the purpose of direct relief-as the minister has just said- and we base that belief upon the following grounds; we have found that, in such and such a year, we needed so much; the next year we needed so much, and last year so much; we believe that $20,000,000 will be sufficient for this purpose this year. Similarly, the amount required for use in the national parks is simply a matter of making up an estimate in that regard. What will be required in other directions is likewise a matter of estimates. That is the way in which parliament proceeds and a ministry presents its estimates. It is idle to say that because no one can foresee what will be required there cannot be some estimate. The method is to present the estimate, give the reasons therefor, and let parliament judge of the soundness of the reasons and exercise its control.
May I point out to the committee what the Prime Minister knows better than anyone else, that, in dealing with questions of great emergency especially where human life is at stake, this House of Commons of Canada has never taken exception to a ministry taking the one course which it can constitutionally take in cases where an appropriation has not been made or is inadequate of asking for a governor general's warrant to meet a particularly emergent situation until parliament can be brought together. I made it very clear at the beginning of the special session in 1930 that, if the ministry found difficulty in estimating what would be required for the purpose of meeting some very critical situation in the matter of relief, and, if it should be necessary, before parliament could be brought together, that a certain expenditure should be made by governor general's warrants on account of the urgency of the human need involved, those of us who sit on this side of the house would take no exception to that particular course, provided that, in the first instance, parliament had been given the control it should have. That is the sound position, and it is the one which ought to be maintained. Are we to hear the same argument again next year, and, if there is a change of government next year, is the incoming government to follow along identical lines in relation to all expenditures concerning unemployment relief? Are we to continue ad-minstering the unemployment relief of the country by means of blank cheques given the ministry by vote of its supporters in the house? There will have to be a halt to that procedure, or we might as well get rid of parliament altogether. No one knows better than do hon. gentlemen opposite that in asking for this continued free hand in the matter of public expenditures, they are taking a course which cannot for a moment be defended.
I must say I believe, whether intentionally or not, the minister wholly misled the House of Commons in the statement he made this afternoon about the $20,000,000. I Certainly got the impression that this year we were going to have, with respect to this particular bill, an amount which would be definite and which would indicate what the ministry really thought would be necessary. Certainly the hon. member for Comox-AIberni had the same impression or he would not have asked of the Prime Minister the question which he did. Indeed, I was waiting until the Prime Minister had concluded his remarks, to ask him the same question: How, if the government cannot foresee what is going to take place in the course of the next few months, has the minister found it possible to fix $20,000,000 as a limit? What is the significance of fixing $20,000,000 as a limit under the circumstances of which we have just been told? It is humbug; humbug pure and simple; no other word would properly describe it. It is another instance of humbug in the case of another great matter which directly affects the Canadian people. Had the minister's statement gone out without a further explanation from him, the people would have been led to believe the government had really got the relief situation in such shape that $20,000,000 would be all that was required.

When I made the statement which I did in this house to the Sermon on the Mount. I was speaking of what I believe, and I said it in all reverence. It ill becomes the Prime Minister of this country to endeavour to provoke a sneer by any reflection on remarks made at that time. I might say, in justice to my right hon. friend, because I think I know him a little better than perhaps he thinks I do, I believe he lost his head a little this afternoon, or he would not have said what he did. I just wish to tell him that, if he does not expect people to be critical of his motives, he had better not impute to others

the motives which have evidently been those that have guided himself.

speechtext:

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Assuming that the minister has given all the information he has at hand-I notice the Prime Minister has now left the chamber; I had hoped to obtain some information from him. When he was speaking this afternoon he took some credit to his government for the fact that no bank in Canada had been obliged to go into liquidation, and for the vast sums of money that he had advanced to the provinces and to the provincial bank in Manitoba. I am not altogether critical of the amounts the government has found it necessary in the past to advance to provincial governments, but I would like to know whether this policy is to continue. Is the federal government to become responsible for all municipalities, all large banking corporations, all insurance companies?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: And Newfoundland.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes, and the Dominion of Newfoundland? That is something that I believe the people of Canada are entitled to know. To what extent are we going to pyramid the liabilities of all parts of Canada? Is the Dominion government accepting full responsibility, no matter who undertakes the obligation, no matter how much a municipality is involved or how much it wishes to spend, no matter what happens to the banks or to the large companies? I say we are entitled to know from this government, now, when they ask us to pass this legislation, to what extent they are prepared to go. I would ask the minister to give us some information in that respect.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The answer, in so far as I can give it, is simply this, that the government is asking the house to invest it with the powers contemplated by the bill, the terms of which are well known to hon. members. They are broad in their character, from some angles, of course. To attempt to prophesy to what extent we may have to invoke the legislation in the coming year is impossible for me or for anyone else. But I think I can say this to the hon.

member, and I do not think he will quarrel much with it, that if during the coming year the occasion arises in connection with the safety of Canada., requiring such measures as are contemplated by this legislation, whether it be loans to provinces, or to business concerns the failure of which would challenge, or imperil or .perhaps destroy the business of this country, then I Should say that this government would take proper action, as contemplated by the legislation sought in this bill, to see that such an occurrence, in so far as it was in the capacity of this government to prevent it, should not take place.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The other night when the minister was dealing with the amount advanced to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for relief, I asked him if he .could tell me what amount was advanced to the Canadian National under like conditions, that is to keep the shops of the Canadian National Railways going intermittently. He promised to get that information for me, and if he has done so I would like to have it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Perhaps I can answer the question in a few words. The Canadian National railway shops were not closed at any time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: No, but they were put on intermittent work.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: So were those of the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian Pacific railway shops were on an even less number of days' work per month than the Canadian National shops. But the Canadian Pacific Railway Company after closing their shops, came to the conclusion that they could not open them again without some 'assistance, and the government, after considering the matter very thoroughly, decided to lend them money to keep the shops open for a certain time last year and a certain time the year before. May I point out that in view of the vast amounts of money which have been advanced from time to time to the Canadian National I do not think there should be criticism of a loan to the Canadian Pacific of, I think, about $2,500,000 in this connection.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Wait until the criticism
is made; I have not yet made any criticism of it. But I think this committee is entitled to know what it costs to keep the Canadian National railway shops open. I will take one example, the shop at Moncton, that is carried on sometimes four days a week; was that carrying on four days a week part of the operating expenses of the Canadian National Railways charged up to deficit?

Relief Act, 1938

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The Canadian National
Railways made no request for assistance in keeping their shops open at any time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
And you have made no
advances to the Canadian National for the purpose of keeping the shops open?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Not for that specific purpose.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
But while the Canadian
National did not make any request for advances, the fact of keeping the shops open to help unemployment was charged against the deficit of the Canadian National Railways Atlantic section?
Mr.- MANION:	I do not admit that, because the Canadian National Railways have never taken the attitude that they kept them open to help unemployment. Their position is that they required to keep them open for the time they kept them open.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I will put it the other way; the Canadian National Railways cut down the time of work in those shops to economize, and practising that economy they were still left with a deficit. That deficit was charged up against the operations of the Canadian National, not paid by the government of the country, and it becomes part of the debt of the Canadian National Railways to the government of Canada. Am I right?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon.
friend is not altogether right in that either, because in the future, if we accept' the Duff report and put it into effect, as we expect to do, the deficit will be charged to the consolidated debt of this country, so it will not be charged as part of the debt of the railway.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Yes, and interest charged
against it. Now I will come to the criticism of the loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The Prime Minister, speaking of that this afternoon, told us that every dollar of the money loaned to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company went to the men, that the shareholders received not one cent, and that the company were to pay back the loan. I was surprised that the Prime Minister at the time did not give the contents of that order in council, which distinctly states that the money was loaned without interest. It further states that it is not to be repaid to the government of Canada until the Canadian Pacific Railway earns sufficient to pay more than five per cent dividends to its shareholders.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Which order in council?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
That is the way the
press reported it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is not only the press report, that is the order in council.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
That is the report I
saw.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
That order in council was
passed, I think, on September 30, 1932. The work was done between September 1 and December 31, 1931.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I am not trying to find
fault, but simply to keep the matter clear. May I suggest that there were two orders in council. One was on a different basis from the other.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I will come to that. I am now dealing with the order passed for the payment of wages to these men for work done between the first of September and the last of December, 1931.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Notwithstanding that that
work was done between those dates, and that parliament sat here from some -time in February to the 29th of June, not one word of information was given to this house, and it was only on the 30th September, 1932, that the order in council was passed, six days before -the opening of the present session. Under that order in council the Canadian Pacific Railway Company received that loan without the payment of one cent of interest, yet in order to make that loan to the Canadian Pacific the government had to issue bonds for $80,000,000, in which amount was included this $1,447,222.70. On that loan to-day we are paying interest at the rate of 4i or 4i per cent. During the flotation of that loan the Caandian Pacific Railway Company subscribed some $3,000,000 on which amount the company is now being paid 4^ per cent interest.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
It is said that this was trust money which was taken from the reserves. That makes no difference; it was Canadian Pacific Railway -money. Where did that reserve come from but from the people of Canada? In part it was built up by the sale of lands with which we bonused the construction of that railway back in 1882. This very rich company is not able to spend $1,500,000 to help out unemployment and keep their men going, though it was able to purchase S3,000,000 of Canadian bonds which are now earning 4i per cent. Further, the conditions under which the loan is to be paid back protect the share-

holders of the company. Under the order in council the loan is not to be paid until the net earnings of the company show sufficient revenue to pay dividends of more than 5 per cent to these rich shareholders.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Rich shareholders?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Yes, most of them are
wealthy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Would the government do the same thing for the farmers?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Will the government do the same thing for the Canadian National Railways?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: We have been doing it for years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: You are charging the Canadian National Radways interest.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: But the interest has never been paid.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The Canadian Pacific Railway Company is not being charged interest. Let me go a little further. I took notice that during his speech to-day the Prime Minister once more felt called upon to attack the press of the country; he referred to rumours in the press which tend to lessen the value of our securities in the United States. Let the right hon. gentleman look at his own speeches; let him refer to the speech he made to the delegation of railway employees who waited upon him three or four weeks ago asking that certain measures be put in force for the relief of rai'lwaymen. If he was correctly reported in the press he recited the dire distress which existed among the employees of the two railway systems of this country; he went on to say that the systems were nearly bankrupt, and he wound up by saying, "I am proud to be able to state to you gentlemen that in my lifetime I predicted this situation."

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: He meant "produced".

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Perhaps so; perhaps the press had the wrong word. What was the result? Within forty-eight hours Canadian Pacific Railway stocks fell several points on the New York market. So instead of blaming the press for rumours depreciating the value of our stocks in the United States the Prime Minister had better strike his breast and say mea culpa.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Before we leave the question of advances to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company there is one other point I should like to bring up. The other evening I referred to an item which appeared in the press to the effect that the Canadian

Pacific Railway Company had been advancing money to railways in the United States which were affiliated with the company, apparently to keep those roads running and to help the men engaged thereon who otherwise were threatened with unemployment. If the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has money that can be used for the purpose of assisting unemployment in the United States surely there was no need for the government to make advances to that company.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend assert that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company advanced money to help unemployment in the United States? I did not know that. I am just asking for information.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: No, I want to know from the Minister of Railways whether he has heard of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company making advances to roads in the United States to assist them in the distressed condition in which they find themselves.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: No, I have never heard that, nor have I seen it in the press. While I am on my feet may I say just a word. I do not wish to delay my colleague's measure, but there was another order in council to which my hon. friend did not refer except in passing. I refer to the second order in council under which the second loan was made. Under the terms of that order in council the money is to be repaid before any dividends are paid.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: But that is not so under the first order in council.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I just wish to keep the record straight in that connection. I do not wish to quarrel with the facts stated by my hon. friend with regard to the first order in council, but under the terms of the second order in council we have insisted that the money must be repaid before any dividends of any kind are paid. I am not here to defend the Canadian Pacific Railway; usually they can defend themselves, but I think in justice to them and in justice to our action in helping them keep their shops open I should say that the company did not pay dividends on common stock at all last year, and I do not think they are likely to pay dividends for some time to come on that stock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The dividends were only postponed for discussion at the next meeting.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
It is not for me to defend the Canadian Pacific Railway, but I do not think that company is likely to pay dividends on its common stock in the very near future.

Relief Act, 1933
I should like to point out also that the shops of that road extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and there were some 8,500 men affected. The Canadian Pacific Railway took the attitude that they could not afford to keep these shops open without some assistance. I do not want to make a comparison between the railways, but for years we have been giving assistance to the Canadian National Railways and I do not think there is anything out of the way in the fact that for two years we have assisted the Canadian Pacific in order to keep these 8.500 men employed. We must remember that in all probability a larger amount than the interest on these loans would have been paid out in direct relief had we not taken this action.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I should like it distinctly understood just what I had in mind; I am afraid the Minister of Railways may have misunderstood me. I do not criticize the lending of the money to help the Canadian Pacific Railway. What I do criticize is the method that was adopted, and I am justified in that criticism by the remarks of the minister. Under the terms of the second order in council the money must be paid back before any dividends are declared; evidently the government saw the folly of their way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: What was the amount of the loan?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if he has any idea of the kind of work in which these 8,500 men were engaged?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I do not know the details, but it was shop work of some kind. I think they called them the back shops, but I am not even sure of that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I received a letter this morning which, had I known this matter was coming up, I woidd have brought with me. I will undertake to show it to the minister perhaps before the day is over. In this letter it is complained that some of the men employed in the Canadian Pacific Railway shops have not received the amount of work they should have received under the money advanced by the government. This is the claim they put forward. Whether it is justified I cannot say, but I hope an investigation will be made. In this communication which they have sent me the men complain that a large part of the money loaned by the government to the Canadian Pacific Railway was used to pay permanent officials who perhaps would otherwise have been employed whether the shops were closed or not. In this way, they say, the Canadian Pacific Railway escaped what were probably ordinary obligations in
using the money to pay permanent officials so that men who ought to have been employed for a longer period were consequently given a shorter term of employment while others had to walk the streets. The Prime Minister this afternoon said that there had been submitted to the government a statement of the wages paid by the Canadian Pacific Railway to the men, and on the basis of the work slips signed by the men an amount of money was advanced to the railway. I have no doubt the Prime Minister's statement was correct, but in view of the letters I received this morning from men actually employed in the workshops I think the Minister of Railways should investigate the matter and see whether the facts are as indicated. The men, I repeat, make the statement that the money advanced by the government to the Canadian Pacific Railway was used to pay officials who would perhaps be employed in any event and that an insufficient sum was used for the purpose of giving employment to the workmen.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I do not believe there is
truth in that statement. Money was borrowed for the purpose of giving employment to men in the shops and I have every reason to believe that it was used for that purpose. Naturally I cannot give details, but I have confidence enough in the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway to believe that they kept faith with the government in that regard. After all it is obviously difficult for men working in the shops to foe able to tell positively what disposal was made of the money borrowed by the railway. It is a common practice among men in the ranks to criticize the officers of the army. It is not necessary that one should go further than the war to find that out. I myself heard severe criticisms from privates who did not know anything about a particular battle front apart from what was going on in their own immediate section; yet they were quite free in their criticisms of headquarters staff. The same is true of workmen generally; they are prone to criticize headquarters. I believe that the Canadian Pacific Railway did with the money exactly what they undertook to do and provided work for the men as far as they could.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I do not think the minister
quite understands the position. In the shops themselves there are a large number of permanent officials. I have worked in the shops so that I have some idea of the situation. In these shops these permanent officials are on a monthly salary and they are the ones in
26S6

Relief Act, 1933
respect of whom the complaint is made. The money was used to pay them instead of a greater proportion of it having been used to give employment to men who had to walk the streets. I will hand on to the minister the communication I have received and I hope he will investigate the matter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I will do that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I regret that the Prime Minister is not in his place because I wish to make a slight comment on a statement he made. I do this for the sake of accuracy, because I think it is essential that we should have a true picture of conditions in the country, neither exaggerated nor underdrawn. In the course of his remarks the Prime Minister congratulated us on the fact that approximately sixty per cent of the farms in Alberta and Manitoba were free from mortgages, only about forty per cent or a little less being mortgaged. I had heard that statement before and I therefore made inquiries and found that my own impression was absolutely correct and that this was not the case. It is true that some sixty per cent of the titles to farms in these provinces are clear of mortgage.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: By acreage or number?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE TEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
By number. But that
does not mean that the title in every case rests with the farmer. It does mot take account of the agreements of sale. The titles to a great many of the farms are held by land-owning companies, such as the railway companies, the Hudson Bay Company, and various land-holding concerns. They are sold to the farmers on agreements of sale and paid for over a term of years, and while the title is clear it is not held by the farmer. So far as the farmer is concerned therefore an agreement of sale is the same thing as a mortgage. I know of my own knowledge-this is not a matter of authentic record however-that the percentage of farms now being paid for under agreements of sale is greater than the percentage of mortgages, so that so far as the farmer himself is concerned, although the statement made by the Prime Minister is technically correct, taking the actual mortgages and the agreements of sale, the percentage is nearer ninety than forty. The Prime Minister's statement is technically correct but it leaves a wrong impression, and nothing is gained by underestimating the situation any more than there is advantage in exaggerating it. It makes no difference to the farmer whether he owns the title and has subsequently borrowed money IMr. Heaps.!
and placed a mortgage on his farm, or whether some land-holding company holds the title and he has to pay under an agreement of sale, for in any event the farm is a mortgaged one. I confirmed my impression by inquiry at the bureau of statistics.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word upon this point before we drift to something else. Right at the outset I want to say that the Dominion government is more responsible for the position in which certain provinces and municipalities now find themselves, that of being unable to meet their bond interest, than anyone else. It is the money policy persisted in and carried out so consistently by this government, the so-called sound money system, which has made it impossible for some of the provinces and municipalities to do their own financing. First of all, this government is responsible for unemployment, and then it insists that the provinces and the municipalities shall bear two-thirds of the burden of unemployment relief. The provinces are forced to borrow money for this unemployment relief, upon which borrowed money they have to pay high interest rates. One of the reasons for these high interest rates is the national service loan which was floated over a year ago. This loan carried a high rate of interest, and the western, and probably the eastern provinces as well, when entering the money market found that they had to pay the highest rates of interest that they had ever paid in their histories. Dominion of Canada bonds are supposed to be the best class of security, and when they carry a high rate of interest the province, the ' municipality or the corporation issuing bonds finds that it has to pay a rate of interest higher than this government. When this national service loan was floated with such1 a high rate of interest other outstanding bonds, amounting to probably billions of dollars, bearing lower rates of interest, immediately dropped in value. Many of these bonds were held by our financial institutions and in order to take care of that situation the government passed an order in council authorizing the banks to value their securities higher than the actual market value.
Let me come back to the government's money policy and the reference made this afternoon by the Prime Minister to the Manitoba savings bank. The right hon. gentleman said that when the government took over the assets of this bank it was found that it had nothing but the I.O.U.'s of the province, and he inferred that those I.O.U.'s were not worth their face value. That was the only inference I could draw from his remarks. If the bonds of the province of Manitoba are not worth their face value it is because that province cannot collect enough in the way of taxes to pay the interest upon those bonds. The reason they cannot collect enough taxes is because the price level of
Relief Act, 1933

agricultural and other products of that province is so low. The reason for these low prices is the unsound money policy of this government which makes the British pound worth only a little over $4. Last year it was down to about S3.70. The government's effort has been to keep down the value of the pound, or keep up the value of the dollar. Had this government adopted a more sensible and fairer money policy, the pound to-day would be worth $4.87, and would have been at least at that value during the past year. The western provinces, and probably some of the eastern provinces, would then have been able to collect several millions of dollars more in taxes. The farmers of Manitoba would have been able to pay the taxes which they have not been able to pay, and which will probably remain unpaid for some time.
I say to the committee that the Dominion government has a great responsibility in assisting the provinces and municipalities. Of course it is a case of how far it can be done; we may come to the point where it cannot be carried any further, but the responsibility rests chiefly with this government. I do not think that we can simply wash our hands of the whole affair and tell the provinces and the municipalities that they must look after their own affairs; it would not be fair. It is ' the unsound money policy of this government which has ruined the credit of some of the provinces and the municipalities, and it will finally ruin the credit of the dominion if it is persisted in too long.

speechtext:
I want to supplement
and enlarge upon what I said yesterday with respect to the back to the land movement. I had not finished when my time was up. I know it is not very popular for a so-called back-bencher to make long speeches, but at the same time it is the duty of a member of parliament to bring as forcibly as he can before the house the situation which he finds in his own section of the country, particularly when it may develop into & national situation.
I said yesterday that I was in favour of the back to the land movement, and that during the last two or three years there has been a reverse movement from the cities hack to the rural centres. There are now tens of thousands of people in our industrial centres who are trying to find useful occupation on the land, and I want to compliment the government for its efforts in that direction.
I want to enlarge particularly upon a certain feature affecting the agricultural class in my own section of the country. Most of them are settlers, and some of them are now graduating into the farmer class. But in that class we find unemployment. Their position is much the same as that of our western farmers in that they are not receiving fair remuneration for their products, particularly for their pulpwood. The government has taken the initiative in bringing these settlers to my own section of the country, and the first crop they will have on their new holding will be pulpwood. It is the only production they will have for a good many years to come. I am sorry to say that the only market which we have for our pulpwood, and this applies to practically all primary products, is the United States, which is now shut to us. I saw a dispatch in this morning's paper that the Prime Minister is going to visit Washington and discuss with the American authorities a larger market for Canadian products in the United States. If this report originating from a press report in England is true, I fervently hope that the Prime Minister will consider the pulpwood question so that we can find a reasonable market for the primary product of the settlers in the newer section of Ontario and elsewhere. It would make the situation all the more easy for the government in maintaining our population on the land.
This winter, under direct relief, which is properly applied in my section under the guidance of Mr. Tackaberry, one of the major

officers of the northern development branch, the settlers on direct relief were paid $2.75 a cord for pulpwood. Anyone who knows anything about the ordinary pulpwood lumbering operations knows that it is absolutely impossible for any Canadian to earn his salt at that rate of pay. The least they should get is $4 or $4.50 a cord. Anyone who knows all the labour involved in cutting a cord, piling it in the bush, hauling it to the siding and loading it on the car, a very hard and slow process, knows that $2.75 a cord is absolutely ridiculous. I know that the government cannot settle this question overnight, but I fervently hope that the Prime Minister, if he visits Washington, will find it possible to open up that market to us. Two years ago he stated in this house that foreign countries had to come to Canada to buy their raw materials. But that does not apply so far as pulpwood is concerned, for our exports of pulpwood in the last three years have been almost nothing, the United States buying most of her supplies from Russia, Finland and other Scandinavian countries. Because of our close proximity to the United States and our railway facilities which place practically all sections of this country within easy reach of it, that is a market which I think should be regained for Canada.
As I said yesterday, we are going to see more and more of the back to the land movement, but at the same time the agricultural class must be helped more than it has been in the past. Under the scheme to which this government contributes, the settler receives a total sum of $600, as was stated by the Minister of Labour the other day, $500 being paid the first year, and the balance of $100 being reserved to take care of the settler in his second year. As I said a moment ago, we have unemployment among the agricultural class in my section of the country. Nearly seventy-five per cent of our own settlers, who have been settled for fifteen or twenty years, are now on direct relief, and unless measures are taken to anticipate the situation within the next two or three years, the back to the land movement will mean that there will be more unemployment. Is there a solution for that difficulty that we can foresee? I answer in the affirmative; yes, there is. I believe it is the duty of the central government to inaugurate a scheme for bonusing land clearing. As the minister knows well, for the last ten or fifteen years we have been agitating in northern Ontario for a land bonus scheme. Last winter, in the Ontario legislature, one of the committees of that house made a recommendation in favour of a land bonusing scheme. The province of Quebec inaugurated

Relief Act, 1933
such a scheme some seven or eight years ago, and I am in a position to know that it has done a lot of good for the northern part of the province. It is absolutely outside of politics. I am glad to be able to support my colleague from North Cochrane, Mr. A. Waters, who spoke in the Ontario house last Monday in favour of such a land bonusing scheme. I hope that the Minister of Labour, who I know has great influence with the government and is well known in every section of northern Ontario, will find it possible to inaugurate such a scheme. It would not take any very large sum of money because, from information I have received from the Department of Agriculture for the province of Quebec, I find that the average yearly expenditure under their scheme for the last three or four years has been 3300,000. I maintain that if we inaugurated such a scheme the people who are now on the land would be absolutely selfsustaining within a very few years.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
When we adjourned at six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was enlarging upon the back to the land movement and suggesting that the government inaugurate in every province of our confederation a land bonusing scheme which is absolutely workable. After giving very thorough study to that sug-53719-171
gestion for many years I believe the amount of the bonus to each family should be $25 per acre per year for not more than ten acres, for land that is Cleared and put under cultivation and seeded. For single men the maximum might be five acres and the bonus $25 per acre per year. Already this scheme is in operation in the province of Quebec, where the maximum amount given is $24, made up of $12 for the clearing of the land to those who actually reside on it and $12 for putting the land under cultivation. This scheme has worked very well in the province of Quebec for the last seven or eight years.
I should like to speak for a moment of the conference held here last winter between the provinces and the dominion I believe the federal government was satisfied with the present policy, and I believe the provinces were looking to this government for direction. I am afraid that direction has not been given, but I hope that before we meet next session some scheme similar to the one I have suggested will have been established by this government instead of the present one of laissez-faire.
This afternoon I said that those taken from the cities and placed on the land under the present scheme have at their disposal a maximum $600, of which $500 is spent in the first year and the other $100 the following year. The man who is placed on new land in Ontario will not be in the same position at the end of his two years as will the same class of man who has been settled on land in Quebec. Under the present scheme of land bonusing in Quebec those people who have taken advantage of the scheme will have at their disposal for the first two years an average of $200 a year, and I think the federal government must realize that the people they are placing on the land now will have to be maintained for more than two years. I say this because I know the real situation in our part of the country. Last fall I read an editorial in the Ottawa Journal praising some financier who had made a speech in this city in which, the Journal claimed, he had stated the situation exactly as it existed so far as finance, industry and commerce were concerned. It is not a pleasant duty for members of parliament to discuss serious situations which may exist in their ridings, but I believe the principle which applies to financial or business men also applies to members of parliament. I am making these statements now not because it gives me any pleasure but because I realize my duty as a member of this house.
Let me urge as strongly as possible that the federal government inaugurate in every sec-

Relief Act, 1933

tioa of the country a system of bonuses, for clearing land in timber areas and for breaking land in the prairie provinces. In addition, in many areas there is a good deal of drainage to be done. The minister is familiar with the northern section of Ontario, and he knows that in a great many cases there is some marsh or muskeg to be drained. We all realize, I know, that when these men leave the cities without capital it is absolutely impossible for them to install a proper drainage system. There again I would urge the federal government to use its influence with the provincial authorities so that certain amounts of money may be given those new settlers who have to drain their land. Every man familiar with agricultural activities fully realizes that unless the land is properly drained there is practically no chance of having good crops. I do not wish to imply that the province of Quebec is leading in all these matters, but in this case I think Quebec is showing the way. In that province a certain amount of money is granted according to the percentage of drainage done on each holding, and I think that principle should be applied in Ontario and the other provinces as well.
During the present session we have heard expounded some very wonderful theories, and when I speak of the back to the land movement I know that I am talking shop. I do believe, however, that in the solution of the present agricultural problem we will find the solution of most of our troubles, I mentioned that fact some time ago, and I should like to enlarge upon that statement, but I believe an opportunity will be afforded me when I speak on the budget. At the same time, this government in cooperation with the provincial and municipal authorities is placing people on the land. These people have been accustomed to highly mechanized surroundings, whether they were working in factories or in other occupations, and we also know that it will be almost impossible for them to get very much machinery for the first few years on the land. Because of that fact alone I want the government fully to realize their responsibility for these people for the next seven or eight years.
The problem of agriculture is the most important problem facing us at the present time. The whole world has been interested in the five year plan experiment in Russia. There the government, which had power over tens of millions of people, decided on certain formulas in order to put that country on an industrial and agricultural basis which would be equal to that of the older and more civilized countries. This was all to be done within five years. I believe the plan has

worked well so far as industry is concerned; they have factories producing machinery, automobiles, farm implements and so on, but if the plan has been a failure

and I believe that in many ways it has been a ghastly failure-it is because of the fact that you cannot conduct agriculture by formulas. In the application of the five year plan they left so much to industry, so much to hydro and so much to other forms of industrial development, while to agriculture they decided on the production of millions of bushels of grain and other commodities. However, such formulas cannot apply to agriculture. Because of drought and climatic conditions that nation to-day is close to starvation; the farming class have not been able to produce what it was thought they would produce. To some extent the same thing applies in our own section of the country to-day.
The movement back to the land is going to increase steadily and I think the government should make a thorough study of the situation. Indeed I think it would be worth while for the provincial and federal governments .to hold a conference to investigate that aspect of the subject alone. That the situation may become serious is indicated by the fact that only a few days ago the hon. member for Stanstead brought the house to a realization that even the committee on agriculture could not deal with all phases of agriculture in every part of the Dominion.
I hope the government will find it possible to remove the anomaly that now exists as between the urban and the rural population in this country. I believe that it is in this direction we should look for a cure for the evils from which we are suffering at the present time.
I will not deal at greater length with the problems that arise under this act. What I stated a week ago I repeat now, namely, that so far .as northern Ontario is concerned we do not believe in the principle of direct relief. It is a palliative, I admit, and the Minister of Labour under present circumstances, seeing that .the federal government has not found it possible to inaugurate a policy of public works so as to give employment to Canadians, no doubt has to maintain this act for another year. I fervently hope however that for the sake of the morale of Canadians, whether urban or rural, the government will find it possible at the end of twelve months to adopt a different system whereby Canadians who are anxious and willing to work may be given employment and not the dole.

Keliej Act, 1933
All the newspapers in northern Ontario, such as the Northern Tribune of Kapuskasing, The Northland Post of Cochrane, and The Porcupine Advance of Timmins, have been decrying this so-called direct relief and asking that the government spend money on capital works. I have been reading an editorial from Saturday Night, which I believe is a journal that is friendly to the present administration. It is the issue of March 4, 1933, and from it I quote the following:
This Country Needs Relief From Relief The state of despair into which we were thrown a few weeks ago by the revelation that the Dominion-provincial conference, of which we had formed high hopes, was not and was never intended to be a serious step towards the solution of any of our economic problems, has lasted until the present time and is still enduring; and under its influence we have, we believe, made practically no reference to any conceivable early alleviation of the country s troubles, save such as may come from the international debt or currency policies of other countries. This silence does not mean that we consider the present state of unemployment relief administration to be any less serious than before; we have merely no hope of anything being done about it. When, therefore, a minister of the crown tries to induce the Canadian people to believe that the problern is solving itself, it is time to protest against that assertion even though we have no expectation that he or his colleagues will do anything to solve it whether we protest or not.
The Hon. W. A. Gordon estimates that Dominion expenditure on relief for the year to March 30 will be below 25 millions. It is possible, though we think not probable, that the amount put through the books may be within that figure; but there is a very heavy lag in the charging of such expenditures against the final guarantor, the Dominion government, and we are convinced that the liability really incurred in the year will be far greater.
This optimistic figure Mr. Gordon compares with that of 41 to 45 millions attained in the preceding year (it is odd, by the way, that the expenditure of a year long since past should still be so vague and that of a year not yet ended so exactly computable), a year in which the method employed was that of financing needed public works instead of the present entirely non-productive "dole." In other words the country got something for most of the 4o millions; while it gets absolutely nothing for its 25 millions; and a considerable part of the 53719-1711
45 millions went not for labour at all but for materials. We are not defending the 1931 system, which we believe was grossly extravagant, but merely pointing out the meaningless nature of such comparisons.
In our section of the country we have had what has been known as the Sturgeon Falls scandal, and the population of that section has come in for a good deal of criticism. In this connection I wish to read the following from an editorial that appeared in the Porcupine Advance of Timmins, of February 2, which places the blame for the present state of affairs there, not on the people of Sturgeon Falls but absolutely on the act itself. I quote:
For some weeks past some of the newspapers of the province have been fairly feasting upon the sensational disclosures in connection with the .administration of direct relief at Sturgeon Falls. Day after day has brought its startling disclosure. And then comes an anti-climax. The people of Sturgeon Falls explain it all by blaming it all upon the newspapers! The newspapers have made a sensation out of inconsequential details, the theory says. The whole thing doesn't amount to anything in particular (so the explanation runs) but the newspapers have made a mountain out of a collection of molehills. Of course, quite a respectable little mountain could be made out of molehills, if you had enough of them,-and there seems to be quite a number of molehills in this Sturgeon Falls business. But after the excitement, sensation, astonishment and alarm created by the evidence in the Sturgeon Falls investigation, such an explanation seems cheap, paltry, common! The Sturgeon Falls folks had given hopes of better things. They had shown inventiveness, originality, and romance, and a fine grasp of the essentials for attracting attention. Why spoil it all by a cheap, time-worn, ancient old wheeze, like saying the newspapers are to blame. That is the excuse of all the cheap fellows, whether politicians or criminals or overtalkative fellows alarmed at their own words. Some day newspapers will demand relief from this sort of thing, but in the meantime, the newspapers are sadly disappointed in the people of Sturgeon Falls. Why not blame it all on direct relief? That would be nearer the mark. Direct relief lowers the morale of the people, fosters fraud, encourages dependence, indolence, chicanery and what have you. The newspapers only told about it all. Direct relief was the father, mother and whole family tree of the evils that have shamed Sturgeon Falls.
That editorial I believe reflects the feelings not only of the people of northern Ontario but of every section of Canada.
There is another matter I want to discuss for a moment or. two. I believe that in connection with this relief measure we are creating another bureaucracy. So far this country has kept itself pretty well away from that danger, but here we are setting up a new set of officials whose duties frequently overlap those of existing officials. In northern Ontario there is an organization that looks after
Relief Act, 1933

the farmers and settlers, and generally speaking the higher officials of that organization enjoy the confidence of the people. Now, I believe that the administration of direct relief should be left in the hands of the northern development branch. There are officials in every locality under this relief measure and personal conflicts are bound to come up, to the detriment of the whole scheme. I know that I am expresing the views of the Conservative member for North Cochrane in the legislature of Ontario, because he made the same statement in the legislature this week, when he urged that the administration of direct relief be left in the hands of the officials of the northern development branch. The Ontario government finds it necessairy to curtail expenditures to some extent in connection with the branch, but it must maintain a skeleton staff, and most of their officials-I could mention many names which are well known to the minister-are men who are fully equipped for the administration of relief. They know the situation thoroughly and are familiar with all the conditions that exist in that part of the country. Why have this overlapping of officials? I am making this suggestion in all sincerity and I hope it will be received in that spirit. I have seen it work out last summer, I have heard of many cases, and I have come to the conclusion that we have too many officials bringing about a conflict in jurisdiction. The provincial government has a splendid body of officials and efficient organizations which cover eighty per cent, of the airea of the province of Ontario. They are fully equipped and have had experience during the present depression, and I feel that their work would be satisfactory to everyone concerned.
I stated last Friday that perhaps we could criticize some of the acts of administration or certain cases here and there where politics had played a part, but taken as a whole I believe that the administration, as far as northern Ontario is concerned, has been carried out without political interference. I hope the minister will find his way clear to cooperate along these lines in the application of the direct relief act. May I again express the hope that the government will find it possible to provide work for many of the men up in our fine section of the country.
My last appeal is that the government devise means whereby in useful and fruitful occupations our people may again come into the full meaning of Canadian nationhood.

When evil days fell upon ancient nations there was generally a famine or a plague of some kind, grasshoppers, locusts or the like. At the present time our country is well favoured by the hand of Providence. We have an abundance of everything, an overabundance, in fact. We have tqo much food, and yet we find starvation in this land. We have too much clothing, and yet some of our people are naked. We have too many houses, and many of our citizens are without homes. We have too much coal, and some of our people are freezing. We have too much of everything that the heart of man can long for, and yet we have a famine-unemployment. Imagine unemployment in a young and rich country like Canada, with its great resources! Nevertheless unemployment is here and getting worse. Let me compare our unemployment figures with those of some other countries. On October 15, 1932, in France one out of 170 was unemployed; in Italy, one out of 45; in Great Britain, one out of 25. Canada-just imagine, in this young and prosperous country!-one out of every twelve of our population is unemployed, according to the Prime Minister's own announcement. They did not realize that high tariffs were not going to improve the traffic on their railway, and the Canadian National men were not much better. How can you improve traffic on the railway by raising the tariff rates three times as high, putting on a six per cent sales tax when the goods come off the cars, and an excise tax of three per cent, and then telling these fellows it will improve traffic on the railway and give employment to more railwaymen? And so we could go from one class to another.
The poor farmer, I pity him. I never knew why they were so much opposed to the New Zealand butter treaty, but there was a little logic and brains behind that opposition. It was a great mistake, as any farmer who looked into it could not fail to realize, when we were getting S3 from New Zealand for every dollar she got from us. The farmers are among the greatest sufferers. Ostensibly they are living in their homes, but it is a sad condition when a man has reached the age of fifty-five, has his family around him and depending on him, and knows that he is not worth a dollar, that if his creditors demanded payment he could not possibly pay them and would have to walk off his farm. That is the condition of many farmers in our good old county of Wellington, where we pride ourselves on good farms and good farmers; yet in some cases their taxes have been unpaid for two years. Yet these are men who three years ago were fairly well off. The previous speaker spoke of poverty in the west. No doubt the western farmer is poverty stricken, but in Ontario the farmers are suffering very seriously from the advice they received from Tory Toronto.

We do not want great banking systems that control our economic power and set up white elephants to advertise themselves like the Bank of Commerce in Toronto-a fool enterprise-instead of lending the money to the farmers in the rural districts. They take the money from the rural parts and spend it foolishly in the cities. We want a banking system from which the small town merchant and the home builder can secure a limited amount of money and credit. We need, as never before in Canada,-and this I think is very important-we need a Magna Charta defining the rights and privileges of the poor classes. The farm and labouring classes are certainly being imposed upon by the policies of this government. Of course the rich wish to keep their fortunes; it is only natural that they wish the payment of bonds to be guaranteed and factories to be kept working-we all want that. They want to keep the banks open and solvent, and we all want that too. But the wishes of the poor take a different direction: they wish work or increased wages-and some of them surely need it. The farmers wish to get a better price for their wheat and wool; the labourer wants work so that he may have enough to eat and to wear and so that he may provide something for his old age.
Now I would like to deal more particularly with the causes of this unemployment. One important factor is the depreciation in the values of the products of the farm, as a result of which farmers are unable to buy. A farmer who bought his farm three years ago for $6,000, giving a mortgage for $3,000, to-day has not a dollar of equity in his farm. The depreciation of farms is at least fifty per cent; the mortgagee literally owns the farm. When he bought that farm, $3,000 perhaps meant 3,000 bushels of wheat, but to-day it means about 7,000 or 8,000 bushels, and the result is a double liability. What has brought about that situation? It has resulted from stangu-lated trade and commerce due to high tariffs, the sales tax, the great expenditures of this government, increased taxation of all kinds and the increase in the national debt. It seems that decreases in trade and increases in taxation go together. I suppose we all realize that the difference in tariff revenues between the last year the Liberal government was in power and the first year the present government took office was about $80,000,000. which had to be made up by taxation. There are about 2,000,000 homes in Canada, which means that $40 would have to be collected from each home to realize that amount. That amount would drive most of our farmers off the la"4

Relief Act, 1933
if they had to pay it in extra taxation. Economic conditions are not known by the public; one after another our Conservative friends stand up and boldly declaim on behalf of their beloved policy of high tariffs, telling the people that good times are just around the corner and that we are on the up grade. We believe they should tell the truth; optimism is not a species of cheerful imbecility based on bedtime stories. We must not forget the statement by Lady Nairne that "truth will stand when all else faileth," and I think the public should be told definitely what is the situation and asked to cooperate in facing it. To-day the people have lost faith, and nothing destroys faith more than falsehood. People are afraid; fear paralyzes their efforts. We must take the people into our confidence and tell them the truth and ask for intelligent cooperation. If we did so we might experience some improvement.
The other day we read in the press that Sir Arthur Currie was pleading for an inflation of the Conservative party by adding to it Liberal brains. Knowing the Curries as I do I felt that he saw a sair, need, and I would say he was one hundred per cent Conservative. You cannot ask for more members on the other side; they have so many now they do not know what to do with them. They have enough material for two cabinets, yet Sir Arthur Currie rightly thinks there should be some Liberal brains infused into the Conservative party, and he is not the only one who so thinks. The country has begun to realize that something like this is absolutely necessary.

I believe he thought he was right, but now he is coming to the point where he knows he is absolutely wrong, and I think his followers are beginning to realize that his policy is carrying this country downhill as fast as we can go. This would not be the case if we were not following the policies of the United States, and they are bigger fools than we are. They have committed all the sins we have committed, but they were a little ahead of

us. We were imitators; we have been mimicking the United States. At one time the capitalists of the United States wanted control of the financial system; they wanted to make and valuate their own money, but Washington said, "No, we are not going to give away our rights". Later on Jefferson said the same thing but when the war came Lincoln sold the rights of the people and allowed United States capitalists to make and valuate their money. Once I attended a celebration on Lincoln's birthday, and much ado was made about Lincoln worshipping the goddess of liberty. I could not help saying that Lincoln liberated the slaves constitutionally but enslaved the inhabitants of the country economically when he tied them up to the financial institutions of the United States and of Great Britain, because at that time Great Britain had an influence over United States banking institutions similar to the influence the United States has over us at the present time.
Now I come to what I think is the great cause of this depression; I refer to deflation and its collateral forces. You can deflate money without destroying it, without taking it out and burning it as the banks do every year when the western crop is moving. Deflation simply means removing money from circulation. I think the definition of the power of money is similar to that law of physics which says that the force of a moving body is the weight of the body multiplied by its velocity. I believe the power of money is the volume of money multiplied by its velocity, and I think the power of money depends more on its velocity than on its volume. Hon. gentlemen to the left keep suggesting that we should increase the volume and inflate money. I am not sure that this has not been done; I think that action has , been taken by the government to the extent of at least $35,000,000, if not more.
The great thing about money, however, is to keep it in circulation. One dollar would pay a thousand dollars of debt if you could keep it going fast enough and in a certain direction. The usual number of moves of a dollar in circulation is ten or fifteen in a year, so one dollar will pay ten dollars' worth of debts and one hundred dollars will pay a thousand dollars' worth of debts. At the present time, however, we feel that instead of increasing the velocity of money the government has strangled trade and commerce so that money cannot circulate. I believe everything that checks the velocity of money or that comes between the producer and the consumer is a deflator, that it will lower the

prices of farms, that it will lower wages and throw men out of employment. I believe that the closer together you can bring the producer and consumer the more you will actually inflate. I think a hill on a railway right of way is a deflator. A storm at sea is a deflator. A cataract on a navigable river is a deflator. These all hinder the commodities of the producer reaching the consumer. Every tariff barrier is a deflator; it reduces the wages of the labourer and throws men out of employment. Time is a deflator; if you can trade your products with some person close at hand it takes less time to make a turnover.

Friday afternoon is usually looked upon as the parliamentary quiet week-end; it is the day that is usually chosen to put through knotty bills, agricultural estimates, difficult resolutions and that sort of thing, but this afternoon has proved to be an exception to the rule in this respect. We had a violent volcanic eruption on the part of the Prime Minister and then a sudden departure; and we have not seen him since. I was going to make the suggestion to the minister who is leading the house-it may be the Minister of Railways at this moment- that as it can be seen by the temper of this committee we are not going to get anything through to-night, they might as well take up something that we might agree on>
and thus save time. If, however, that is not considered advisable, I shall proceed.
What was the cause of the gaseous eruption we had this afternoon on the part of the Prime Minister? The Minister of Immigration and some other portfolies, in explaining this resolution, said that an amendment was to be made to the bill based on the resolution when the bill came before the house, and it was a very important amendment inasmuch as it meant reverting to the good old practice of responsible government and supervision of all expenditures by parliament. This is something that has been fought for by the Liberal party for nearly a hundred years and won, and for the first time departed from by this government. Does anybody think our right hon. leader, who has been noted ever since this government came into power for fighting first for the retention of that right and afterwards for the restoration of it, could, when he sees it restored, ignore the change? He could not lightly pass that up. Nobody would expect anyone in the position that my right hon. leader occupies would have let that pass without some comment. What was the comment? I have not read Hansard since, though I might have done so, but I recall quite well that no offensive language was used in making the criticism, nor was the tone offensive. In fact, the observation was particularly mild when one considers that after three years my right hon. leader has attained his objective with respect to this important matter. Yet the Prime Minister did not seem to take it in that way. I did not dream of such an eruption and explosion as a result of the fair comment of my leader. Well, it came, I suppose all of us have bad days and this may have been one of the Prime Minister's. He apparently got up on the wrong side of the bed. Those of us who have been in cabinets and know how tired* we sometimes are

towards the end of the week realize the situation. An important railway bill is coming before the house on Monday and I would rather have been in a quiet frame of mind for it; but I feel we on this side have had just cause for indignation, and in the absence of the Prime Minister we are precluded from going into the matter in the way we should.
I want to commend the minister now, and I hope I can do it without any further irruptions from the treasury benches, for having reverted to the policy of having at least part of the expenditures under this bill discussed in this house. Will the minister tell us how he arrives at that $20,000,000?
In extenuation of or excuse for the arbitrary blank cheque method of administering public moneys which this government has been practising for the last two years, the Prime Minister this afternoon made a lot of the fact that no individual could estimate the requirements of the country and specify any definite amount that would be required for relief. But you can say that of any vote in the estimates. As my right hon. leader has pointed out times without number, the Prime Minister might mention any amount he liked and my leader would let it go, and if the amount designated were not enough, the usual practice of resorting to governor general's warrants would meet any further situation that might arise. So there was no justification for departing from the regular practice of the supervision of all government expenditures by this parliament, instead of playing the dictator, mighty unsuccessfully too in this respect, until now the proper pra.ctioe is about to be resorted to.
What is the trouble then, with the Prime Minister? I know it is hard to climb down. Don't we remember in this house the night the special income tax bill was climbed down from and the booby talk that was indulged in by the Prime Minister? The coon came down, however. We do not know or care whether it was head first or tail first, but he came down, and he has had to come down many times since, and will have to many times more, and the sooner the Prime Minister learns how to back away from his many blunders the better it will be for this country. He had not the grace to climb down properly and gracefully this afternoon, but instead he blew off like an extinct volcano come to life again. He has been an extinct volcano for the last month. I thought his colleagues were bringing him up, like Maggie was bringing up Jiggs, making him behave better. But even if Maggie were successful for a while Jiggs still blows off now and again as he did this afternoon. We do not want any more of that, Mr. Chairman. We do not mind it once. We do not mind having some consideration for the Prime Minister and his colleagues in their troubles in trying to bring him up, while he is trying to bring them up. Has there been one thing that they have put their hand to that they have not made a botch of in the last two years? I do not know one. They could not come down on this policy of parliamentary control of money without making a mess of it also. If the Minister of Labour had been left to himself I think he would have acted all right. He is a ponderous gentleman but
Relief Act, 1933

I think he is a pretty good scout taken on the whole. I do not know how he came to speak of the amendment on the resolution, but since he spoke about it I presume I am also in order, Mr. Chairman, although I think he should have waited till the bill came down.
Anyway, the government has made many blunders, and the Prime Minister has not yet learned how to back down in spite of all his experience in that respect. He will have to learn soon because the way is thorny and strewn with many back-ups, and I am sure that the government will have to get a fresh pair of breeching straps on because the other ones are all worn out by this time with backing up and backing up from the sight of themselves and their evil works. Our good friend the Minister of Labour, with his more phlegmatic character, and not so much like a spirited racehorse, does not mind it so much. But they have got to do it just the same.
There are one or two other matters to which I wish to refer. The Prime Minister was continually complaining that there was no way of estimating the nature of the crop or the nature of the climate next year. Then how was this $20,000,000 estimated? The summer and fall there were exceptionally dry, the winter has been dry; there has been no snow or very little. The cars are running from Weyburn to Moose Jaw yet. If they can do that now, why not at other times? Has there been some new knowledge of meteorological conditions whereby you can forecast the rainfall for next summer? I never heard of any such new information, but if the minister has any, I wish he would tell us upon what he bases this estimate for the coming summer. If he cannot tell us, then all this fumadiddle nonsense the Prime Minister was indulging in, because that is what it was, goes by the board.

Daniel, in southern Saskatchewan, and he would get better information even from that partisan source.
